name: Angola
summary: Before departure, the Angolan consulate in the country of death reviews a transfer (trasladação) file: legalised death certificate, transport permit from the local authority and a health certificate. The casket then travels with these originals to Luanda.
documents: Full death certificate, legalised by the foreign ministry of the country of death (Lisbon consulate: issued within the last 6 months)
Transport/transfer permit issued by the local authority of the country of death (in Portugal: PSP 'alvara de trasladacao'), legalised
Medical health certificate (atestado medico sanitario), legalised
Portuguese translations by an official translator where documents are in another language (practice of the London consulate)
coffin: Not published by Angolan authorities. A hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case is the international standard and should be expected; confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Not specified in official Angolan sources found; embalming is normally performed for long-haul transfer. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: The Angolan Consulate General (e.g. Lisbon, London) handles the trasladacao request. Lisbon lists legalisation of each document by the foreign ministry of the country of death; London requires official Portuguese translation, notarisation and foreign-office authentication before consular authentication. Lisbon states 8 working days, no fee. The consulate may ask for extra documents or an interview.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Luanda airport; a funeral agent collects the casket. No legal burial deadline was found; funerals in Angola usually take place quickly. A 2017 tariff revision reportedly exempts coffins from customs duty (press report, unverified).
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket.
private_jet_note: Arrive at Luanda (or another customs airport) with the consular file approved before take-off.
export: The next of kin instructs a funeral agent, who registers the death with the Angolan Civil Registration Office (can take some time) and handles local procedures. Sudden, accidental or suspicious deaths involve the police and Public Prosecutor; post-mortem reports may take months. No legal timescale for repatriation. Mortuary standards vary; only one crematorium (Luanda).
export_points: Funeral agent needs the next of kin's signed authority
Death registration at the Civil Registration Office is mandatory
Prosecutor inquiry can delay release in unnatural deaths
One crematorium only, in Luanda

at_a_glance.arrival: Customs and health clearance in Luanda

steps.what: Register the death locally and obtain the full death certificate and medical health certificate.
Obtain the local transport permit (e.g. PSP alvara in Portugal) and have all documents legalised and translated into Portuguese.
File the trasladacao request at the Angolan consulate with originals and copies.
Consulate processes the file (Lisbon: 8 working days, no fee).
Casket sealed by the funeral director and flown with the original documents.
Customs and health clearance in Luanda; local funeral agent collects the casket.

key_points: Every document must be legalised; missing papers can lead to refusal
Allow about 8 working days at the consulate
Casket specifications are not published: confirm with the consulate
Not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement on the transfer of corpses, so a laissez-passer alone does not suffice.
authority: Consulates of the Republic of Angola (Ministry of External Relations, MIREX)

Consular authorisation from the Beninese mission (to be confirmed)
coffin: Not published for entry. For exit, the UK government describes a galvanised tin coffin with a special filter inside a strong packing case; expect the same standard for entry.
embalming: Not published for entry; UK guidance states bodies are embalmed before leaving Benin, so embalming should be expected.
consular: Not published. The Beninese consulate (e.g. Consulate General in Paris) is the contact for civil status documents and any transfer authorisation; confirm requirements and legalisation.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Cotonou airport; a local funeral director collects. No official burial deadline found.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. private_jet_note: Confirm entry documents with the Beninese consulate before departure.

name: Botswana
summary: By law, no dead body may be brought into Botswana without a prior permit from the Minister of Health. The application must describe the deceased, cause of death, transport, health precautions and place of burial, with a medical cause-of-death certificate.
documents: Import permit from the Minister (Ministry of Health), obtained before arrival
Medical certificate of the cause of death (or certified copy)
Certificate that the death was not from a contagious/epidemic disease
Import/export permit from the Botswana Unified Revenue Service (BURS), as reported by government in 2022
coffin: The Act requires an unburied body not in cold storage to be in a strong hermetically sealed sheet-metal shell inside a stout wooden coffin, or else carefully embalmed. Exhumed remains must be sealed in a sheet-metal shell in a wooden coffin. The permit may impose further conditions.
embalming: Embalming certificate listed among required documents (government statement, 2022). The Act accepts embalming as an alternative to a sealed metal shell for keeping bodies.
consular: The application is addressed to the Minister; Botswana missions abroad help families coordinate with local authorities. Government said in 2022 it has no standing repatriation policy, so requirements may be set case by case.
arrival: Customs clearance (BURS permit) and health checks on arrival; a local undertaker collects. Exhumed remains can only be imported at least 2 years after burial (4 years for infectious disease deaths). Ashes do not need a permit.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket. The ministerial import permit must be obtained before the body enters Botswana, whatever the type of flight.
private_jet_note: Ministerial import permit required before the flight; bring the BURS permit for customs.
export: Removal from Botswana also needs a permit from the Minister, with the cause-of-death certificate and written approval from the authorities of the destination country. UK guidance lists death certificate, passport copy, embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer. Deaths should be registered within 30 days; certificates are in English.
export_points: Minister's removal permit required
Destination country's written approval must be attached
Embalming certificate and transfer certificate
Ashes need no permit

at_a_glance.coffin: Sealed metal shell in wooden coffin
at_a_glance.permit: Ministry of Health permit before arrival

steps.what: Collect the death and cause-of-death certificates and a non-contagious disease certificate.
Apply to the Minister of Health for the import permit, stating transport, precautions and burial place.
Embalming and sealing in a metal-lined coffin by the funeral director.
Receive the import permit and obtain the BURS import permit.
Customs and health clearance; a local undertaker collects for burial.

key_points: Statutory permit required to bring a body in (Conveyance of Dead Bodies Act)
Ashes do not need a permit
Exhumed remains: minimum 2 years after burial
Not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement on the transfer of corpses, so a laissez-passer alone does not suffice.
authority: Minister of Health (Conveyance of Dead Bodies Act, Cap. 65:01); BURS for customs

name: Cameroon
summary: A Certificate of Repatriation (mortuary laissez-passer) must be obtained from the Cameroonian embassy or high commission in the country of death, applied for and paid on the evisacam.cm portal. The UK mission also requires a regional authorisation signed by the Prefect for entry into Douala or Yaounde.
documents: Request letter addressed to the Ambassador / High Commissioner
Death certificate (English or French translation if needed)
Deceased's passport or Cameroonian ID, birth certificate
Authorisation to remove the body from the country of death
Burial permit and regional authorisation from the Service of Social and Cultural Affairs (Centre or Littoral), signed by the Prefect (UK mission)
Funeral company details, flight ticket copy if available (Germany mission)
coffin: Not detailed by the missions whose pages were opened. A sealed zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case should be expected; some missions reportedly also ask for a photo of the empty casket and a funeral-home statement that it contains only the body.
consular: Certificate of Repatriation / mortuary laissez-passer issued by the Cameroonian mission; documents uploaded and fee paid online at evisacam.cm (Laissez-Passer section). Fee example: Germany EUR 153, non-refundable. The death certificate issued by the Tokyo embassy is free. Without the Prefect's regional authorisation the UK mission may not issue the certificate.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at Douala or Yaounde-Nsimalen; the family or funeral home collects. The regional authorisation covers transfer into the region. No burial deadline published.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket. The consular Certificate of Repatriation and the regional authorisation must be obtained before departure.
private_jet_note: Consular laissez-passer via evisacam.cm and Prefect's authorisation needed before take-off.
export: A funeral home obtains authorisation to repatriate the body. Needed: death certificate (after hospital registration), cause-of-death certificate (usually within a week), post-mortem report if death outside hospital, passport. Embalming offered by funeral homes. Autopsy reports can take long. UK guidance cites about GBP 2,000 for repatriation to the UK (estimate).
export_points: Funeral home obtains the repatriation authorisation
Cause-of-death certificate usually within a week
Agree costs in writing beforehand
Autopsy reports can be slow
